statement: In language there are only differences without positive terms: a sign's meaning is what it is not, its borders drawn by neighbouring words, and its identity is a position in a system of oppositions — as a chess piece is nothing but its value in the game, unaffected by being recast in marble.

name: The sign
statement: The linguistic sign is two-sided — a signifier (the perceivable sound-image) and a signified (the concept) — with the referent, the actual thing, outside the sign entirely, bracketed by Saussure.

name: Meaning versus reference
statement: Separating meaning from reference makes the structural method possible: meaning can be studied as a closed game, as chess can be studied without regard to what the pieces are made of.

name: Self-grounding system
statement: The system of meanings is self-grounding and circular: every word is defined by other words with no non-linguistic base case, so meaning is internal to the system, position against position, all the way down, like a geometry that touches no ground outside itself.

name: Pointing cannot fix meaning
statement: Pointing at a thing cannot fix a word's meaning, because the gesture cannot specify which cut is meant — the dog, the animal, the mammal, the pet, the breed — and most of language has nothing to point at.

name: The system precedes the speaker
statement: No speaker assembles the linguistic system bottom-up; every speaker acquires an already-finished system that was in place before they existed, so what acquisition delivers is a position in the network, not a stash of associations.

name: The 'I' is spoken by language
statement: Whatever 'you' are, meaning-wise, you are made of inherited linguistic material; the 'I' that believes it speaks language is first something spoken by it, and one cannot mean anything, even in rebellion, except out of material that was already there.
aliases: the I that believes it speaks language is, first, something spoken by it

name: Selection and combination
statement: Every act of speaking simultaneously selects a word from the set of words that could occupy the slot and combines the chosen word with its neighbours into a sequence; selection and combination are the two axes on which every sentence rides.

name: Metaphor and metonymy
statement: The selection pole does its creative work as metaphor — naming a thing by something similar to it — and the combination pole as metonymy — naming a thing by something adjacent to it.

name: Aphasic dissociation of the poles
statement: Some aphasias destroy the selection pole, leaving patients able only to chain words by contiguity, while others destroy the combination pole, leaving only substitution without any sentence — showing that selection and combination are two separate machineries.

name: The two operations are the two poles
statement: The unconscious's two operations line up with language's two poles: condensation fuses several thoughts into one image, which is substitution on the basis of similarity (metaphor), and displacement moves charge onto a neighbouring trivial element, which is substitution on the basis of contiguity (metonymy).

name: Two fundamental dream-work operations
statement: Freud holds condensation and displacement to be the two fundamental operations of the dream-work — the machinery itself; the remaining distortions (staging, secondary revision) presuppose them, and secondary revision is the waking mind's after-the-fact edit rather than unconscious machinery.

name: Condensation is metaphor
statement: Condensation is metaphor: several thoughts are fused into a single image, one figure substituted for a whole network of thoughts because it resembles all of them at once.

name: Displacement is metonymy
statement: Displacement is metonymy: the charge of an unbearable thought slides along the chain of associations onto a trivial neighboring element, so that contiguity itself stands in for the thing, as 'the Crown' stands in for the monarchy.

name: The unconscious runs on the signifier
statement: The unconscious selects by the material signifier — sounds, letters, words as things — and is indifferent to the signified (the meaning it bears); it operates on the letter, as when a patient is tormented by cabbages over her rival Frau Kohl (Kohl = cabbage) or Dora's dream turns on 'jewel box.'

name: Dream as rebus
statement: The dream is a rebus — a picture-puzzle whose elements stand for words — and is therefore something to be read, not seen through.

name: Lacan's algorithm of the sign
statement: Lacan rewrites the Saussurean sign as capital S over small s separated by a bar: the capitalized signifier leads (the machinery runs top-down from the material sound), the bar is a resistance rather than a bond, and the signified is not a partner but an effect produced late as the chain runs and never finally fixed.

name: Cogito
statement: Descartes' cogito: radical doubt cannot doubt the occurrence of thinking itself, since doubting is an instance of thinking; cogitatio ('thinking') covers the whole stream of experience — sensing, seeming, feeling, willing, doubting — so that in the act of thinking the 'I' is present to itself, and this self-transparency is the indubitable foundation on which knowledge is rebuilt.

name: I think where I am not
statement: Lacan's inversion of the cogito: 'I think where I am not; therefore I am where I do not think' — the thinking that is most one's own (the dream-work, the slip, the other scene) runs where one is not present, while the place where one is present to oneself (the ego) is precisely where no such thinking occurs.

name: The split subject
statement: The subject is not the transparent res cogitans but a split: divided between the 'I' that speaks and the circuit that speaks in it; the subject is neither the ego-image nor the unconscious machinery but the barred, proxy-structure between them, and it is split, not eliminated.

name: Signifier represents the subject for another signifier
statement: A signifier represents the subject for another signifier: the subject appears only by proxy, as a position in the signifying chain, never in person — as a knight is nothing but its position in the game; the word 'I' is the sharpest case, the language's word that never coincides with the one who speaks it.

name: The one bar
statement: The bar is a single operator marking the same structural fact in two places — in S/s it marks that the material form is cut off from any natural presence of its meaning, and in $ it marks that the subject is cut off from any present self that could coincide with its representation; both bars say that no transparency crosses the line.

name: The Symbolic
statement: The Symbolic is the register comprising everything that exists only as a position within a system — language, law, kinship, money, roles — which produces real effects (a banknote buys bread, a signed paper marries you) while existing nowhere in particular, since it is relative to positions and precedes and outlasts every individual.

name: The big Other
statement: The big Other (A, Autre) is the Symbolic order personified as a place — the place from which one is spoken and the addressee-of-last-resort, the structure itself standing in the position of guarantor rather than any person, God, or government; even a private conversation or a mathematical proof is structurally a message addressed to the Other.

name: Discourse of the Other
statement: The unconscious is the discourse of the Other: because the circuit that speaks where one is not speaks in signifiers, the very material of one's unconscious is the Other's borrowed material.

name: The little other
statement: The little other (a) is the person in front of you — rival, beloved, the mirror — the two-person register of the Imaginary; the big Other is the third that was always already there, the frame the dyad stands in.

name: Information Principle
statement: The entire information content of a database is represented in one and only one way: as explicit values at named attribute positions in rows — no fact may live in pointer structure, row position, or any hidden channel; if it is in the database, it is a value in a cell.
aliases: The entire information content of the database is represented in one and only one way: as explicit values at named attribute positions in rows

name: Pointer vs. value
statement: A pointer's meaning lives outside the data — valid only within one process's memory layout at one moment — so pointer-based data loses the facts it encodes when written to disk, loaded into another program, or moved in memory, whereas a self-meaningful value such as customer_id = 3 designates the same thing for every reader, everywhere and forever.

name: Position is not information
statement: Every cell is addressed as (row, attribute name), never by offset or by structure; a fact that exists only as a position — of a row or of a cell — is not in the database at all, only in the reader's head or in the storage layout.

name: First normal form
statement: One value per cell is constitutive of being a relation, not a rung on a design-quality ladder: a list stored in a single cell smuggles positional meaning ('secondness') outside the value layer, which the Information Principle forbids, so every real relation satisfies first normal form by construction.
aliases: 1NF is the model's floor, not a rung on a quality ladder

name: Value equality as the connective mechanism
statement: Because the model has no pointers, when two rows must connect, equality of values is the only connective mechanism the model has.

name: Repeating-group representation
statement: When one thing has many of something, the model represents it as one fact per cell across separate rows with the shared identifier repeated as a value on each row — the shape that recurs as the foreign-key and junction-table patterns.

name: Relation as set of tuples
statement: A relation is a set of tuples, where a tuple is one value assigned to each named attribute (one row's worth of cells); 'set' means identity is by value — two things are equal iff all their values are equal — duplicates collapse into one, and order is meaningless.
aliases: A relation is a set of tuples

name: Heading and domain
statement: A relation's heading is its attribute names each paired with a domain — the set of values that attribute may draw from — and every attribute draws from exactly one domain.

name: No duplicate tuples
statement: If two candidate rows agree on every attribute value they are not two rows but one fact, so a relation can never contain duplicate tuples.

name: Full attribute set always identifies
statement: The full attribute set of a relation always identifies a tuple, because two tuples that agreed on every attribute would be the same tuple.

name: Equality within a domain
statement: Equality comparison is well-defined only between values of the same domain; comparing an amount against a customer name is a category error, not a false statement.

name: Attribute domains enable value comparison
statement: Typing every attribute to exactly one domain is what makes value-comparison well-defined, and value-comparison is what every connection in the model — keys and joins alike — is built from.

name: Superkey
statement: A superkey is an attribute set that identifies every tuple in every possible state — no two tuples ever agree on all of its attributes; 'in every possible state' makes it a claim, not a survey of the rows currently present.

name: Candidate key
statement: A candidate key is a superkey with no removable attribute — drop any one of its attributes and it stops being a superkey; minimality means nothing sparer works (removability, not fewest attributes), so candidate keys of different sizes can coexist. A key is a set of attributes, possibly of size one, and a key of several attributes is a composite key.
aliases: a superkey with no removable attribute

name: Key existence is a theorem
statement: Every relation has at least one candidate key: its full attribute set is a superkey, and removing attributes until identification dies must stop at a candidate key — so key existence follows from set-hood rather than being a rule the model imposes.

name: Primary key as designation
statement: Primary key is a designation, not a different kind of thing: choosing one of several candidate keys as primary is convention, and its real content is announcing which attributes the schema treats as the relation's identifier and having the database enforce that claim by rejecting any insert that would repeat the attribute combination.

name: SQL PRIMARY KEY and UNIQUE
statement: The model has one notion, the candidate key; SQL splits the job into PRIMARY KEY (the designated key, meaning UNIQUE + NOT NULL) and UNIQUE (how every other candidate key is enforced), so all key claims are enforced even though only one gets the title.

name: UNIQUE and NULL
statement: In standard SQL, UNIQUE permits repeated NULLs (NULL is not equal to anything, itself included), so a nullable column cannot serve as a real key in practice — a SQL wrinkle, not a model one.

name: Functional dependency
statement: For attribute sets X and Y of a relation R, the functional dependency X → Y holds iff in every valid state of R, any two tuples that agree on all attributes of X also agree on all attributes of Y — the value of X fixes the value of Y in every state the relation may take, not merely the rows seen so far.
aliases: the value of X fixes the value of Y

name: Key as strongest functional dependency
statement: A key is the strongest special case of a functional dependency: X is a superkey exactly when X → every attribute of R, a candidate key is the same with nothing removable from X, and a general FD is X → Y for some attribute set Y.

name: Direction of a functional dependency
statement: A functional dependency is an arrow, not an equation: X → Y says nothing about Y → X, so each direction must be established as its own fact about the domain.

name: SQL cannot enforce general FDs
statement: SQL cannot enforce a general functional dependency: its constraint vocabulary covers keys, foreign references, and row-local CHECKs, but 'same X, same Y' spans multiple rows, which no mainstream engine lets a check reach.

name: Decomposition
statement: To enforce a general functional dependency X → Y that SQL cannot constrain, a designer moves Y into a table where X is a key; storing each determined fact where its determinant is minimal is decomposition, and it is the entire content of the normal forms.

name: Hidden system identifier
statement: A hidden system-generated row identifier is a physical row address invisible to the data model; because its meaning lives outside the value layer, using it to distinguish rows rebuilds the forbidden pointer and violates the Information Principle.

name: Identity as a visible value column
statement: When two rows must be distinguished, the model's answer is a value column (a purchase_id, a receipt number, or a sufficiently fine timestamp), not a hidden identifier, so that the rows differ by value and set-hood is preserved.

name: Relation, tuple, attribute vs. table, row, column
statement: In the relational model a relation is a table, a tuple is a row, and an attribute is a column; SQL kept the table/row/column vocabulary while the theory kept relation/tuple/attribute.

name: Vector space (over ℝ)
statement: A vector space over ℝ is a set V equipped with an addition u+v∈V and a scaling cv∈V (c∈ℝ) satisfying eight laws: (1) u+v=v+u, (2) (u+v)+w=u+(v+w), (3) a zero element with v+0=v, (4) every v has a negative with v+(−v)=0, (5) 1v=v, (6) (cd)v=c(dv), (7) c(u+v)=cu+cv, (8) (c+d)v=cv+dv.
aliases: a set with two operations — addition of elements and scaling by numbers — satisfying the eight vector-space laws

name: Abelian group plus compatible scaling
statement: The eight vector-space laws compress into exactly two ideas: laws 1–4 say (V,+) is an abelian group (commutative, associative, with a zero and negatives), and laws 5–8 say the scaling respects that group structure by composing and distributing; 'linearity of the operations' means precisely laws 5–8.
aliases: (V,+) is an abelian group and scaling respects that group structure

name: Linear-combination fuel
statement: A vector space's two operations and eight laws are exactly what a linear combination v=c1v1+⋯+ckvk consumes; forming combinations uses nothing beyond addition and scaling.
aliases: linear combinations burn nothing but addition and scaling

name: Transfer of combination-based results
statement: Every concept built from linear combinations (span, independence, basis) and every theorem proved about them transfers intact to any set that supplies two operations satisfying the eight laws — ℝⁿ, matrices, polynomials, functions — so demanding more structure would only shrink the roster of examples without proving anything extra.

name: Element multiplication is undefined
statement: In a vector space, multiplication of two elements is not optional but undefined — the expression xy has no meaning — so the question 'does every nonzero element have a multiplicative inverse?' is not answered no but is unaskable until extra structure (a field or algebra) is installed on top.
aliases: a vector space's elements form a group under addition, where inverse means negative; multiplicative inverses are a field concept with no counterpart here

name: Laws decide membership
statement: Vector-space membership is decided by the eight laws alone, not by the familiarity of an operation's name: operations with unfamiliar names — e.g. 'addition' x⊕y=xy and 'scaling' c⊙x=xᶜ on the positive reals — form a vector space exactly when they satisfy the laws, so the decision procedure is a cheapest-first checklist (closure under both operations, then zero, then negatives, then the scaling laws) rather than intuition.
aliases: the eight laws do not care what the operations look like
selecting by the familiarity of an operation's name instead of by the eight laws is the failure mode

name: Arithmetic laws are identities
statement: The six arithmetic vector-space laws are identities — each asserts the equality of two expressions built from elements — so when those expressions are computed with the same operations they hold automatically in any subset of V, and an identity cannot know that a subset exists; only the possibility of an operation leaving the subset is genuinely new.
aliases: an identity cannot know that W exists

name: Subspace test
statement: A subset W of a vector space V is itself a vector space under the same operations exactly when it is nonempty, closed under addition, and closed under scaling; checking 0∈W first is a useful one-line canary that disqualifies failures instantly but is not an independent requirement.
aliases: nonempty, closed under addition, closed under scaling

name: Closure manufactures zero and negatives
statement: Within a subspace, closure under scaling alone produces the zero and the negatives: 0=0w∈W and −w=(−1)w∈W for any w∈W, so zero and negatives need not be checked separately.

name: Linear condition
statement: A linear condition is a statement L(v)=0 where L is additive (L(u+v)=L(u)+L(v)) and homogeneous (L(cv)=cL(v)) — i.e. a weighted sum of the coordinates and nothing more.
aliases: L(v)=0 with L additive and homogeneous

name: Solutions of a homogeneous linear condition form a subspace
statement: The solution set of a homogeneous linear condition L(v)=0 is a subspace, because L is linear: L(u+v)=L(u)+L(v)=0+0=0 and L(cv)=cL(v)=0; but the same condition set equal to a nonzero constant, L(v)=1, is an affine slice — a translate of a subspace — never a subspace, since L(u+v)=1+1=2 escapes immediately.
aliases: homogeneous linear condition → subspace; nonzero constant → affine slice
a linear condition set equal to a nonzero constant is a translate of a subspace

name: Nonlinear conditions fail closure
statement: A condition that is nonlinear in the entries is not a subspace: {det A=0} fails closure because diag(1,0)+diag(0,1)=I with det I=1≠0 — two singular matrices summing to an invertible one — consistent with det being degree 2 in the entries, so no linearity is available to save closure.
aliases: two singular matrices summing to an invertible one

name: Canonical vector spaces inherit laws from ℝ
statement: ℝⁿ (componentwise operations), ℝ^{m×n} matrices (entrywise: (A+B)_{ij}=a_{ij}+b_{ij}, (cA)_{ij}=c·a_{ij}), polynomials (coefficientwise), and functions ℝ→ℝ (pointwise: (f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x), (cf)(x)=c·f(x)) are all vector spaces; each of the eight laws is verified entry by entry and reduces to a law of real numbers, so these coordinatewise structures inherit their laws from ℝ, and each is an abelian group under its addition because (ℝ,+) is.
aliases: coordinatewise structures inherit their laws from ℝ
one proof for all four rows at once

name: Matrix multiplication is extra structure
statement: Matrix multiplication is not the addition of the matrix vector space but extra structure nowhere mentioned in the eight laws; judged as an addition it fails immediately, since AB≠BA in general, its identity is I rather than the zero matrix, AB can be the zero matrix with both factors nonzero, and most matrices have no multiplicative inverse.
aliases: matrix multiplication is present only when explicitly written; the vector-space operations are entrywise

name: Matrix as point and as action
statement: A matrix has two faces that are the same object: a point in a vector space (an m×n matrix is mn independent coordinates, its entries, freely added and scaled entrywise) and an action (rows times columns, transforming vectors) — and the subject's power comes from switching between them, using the entry face for structure and counting and the action face for transformation.
aliases: the two faces of a matrix

name: Every matrix-work subspace is a null space
statement: In matrix work, every subspace encountered is a null space in disguise — the solution set of some A x = 0 — because such solution sets are exactly the homogeneous linear conditions on the coordinates.
aliases: every subspace you meet is a null space in disguise

name: Digitalisation amplifies ICT risk
statement: Increased digitalisation and interconnectedness of financial entities amplify ICT risk, making the financial system more vulnerable to cyber threats and ICT disruptions.

name: ICT interdependencies as systemic vulnerability
statement: Interconnectedness of financial entities and their ICT systems is a systemic vulnerability, because localised cyber incidents can spread quickly across the financial system regardless of geographical boundaries, potentially causing liquidity runs and loss of confidence in financial markets.

name: Digital resilience gap in financial regulation
statement: Post-2008 financial reforms focused on financial resilience, so ICT security and digital resilience, though part of operational risk, remained unevenly and incompletely addressed in Union financial regulation.

name: Fragmentation harms internal market
statement: Divergent national rules and gaps or overlaps in ICT risk provisions, such as incident reporting and resilience testing, obstruct cross-border financial services, distort competition and impose cost-ineffective compliance, especially since technology risks have no borders.

name: Need for harmonised digital resilience rules
statement: Further harmonisation of key digital operational resilience requirements for all financial entities is required, extending the Single Rulebook and supervision to ICT risk, to preserve financial stability and market integrity and protect investors and consumers.

name: Qualitative ICT risk rules over capital
statement: Prior operational risk rules favoured capital requirements for ICT risk rather than qualitative rules on protection, detection, containment, recovery and repair, reporting and testing; Regulation 2022/2554 consolidates and upgrades these in one act covering ICT risk management, incident reporting, resilience testing and third-party risk monitoring.

name: Choice of a Regulation
statement: A Regulation, based on Article 114 TFEU, is the most appropriate instrument for the digital resilience framework because it reduces regulatory complexity, fosters supervisory convergence, increases legal certainty and limits compliance costs and competitive distortions.

name: Proportionate principle-based approach
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, financial entities follow the same principle-based ICT risk rules, applied in light of their size, risk profile and the nature, scale and complexity of their activities; this consistency strengthens confidence and stability.

name: Lex specialis to NIS2
statement: Regulation 2022/2554 is lex specialis with regard to Directive (EU) 2022/2555 because it imposes more stringent ICT risk management and incident reporting requirements; financial entities nonetheless remain part of that Directive's ecosystem, with cooperation between financial supervisors, CSIRTs and Cooperation Group.

name: Single incident reporting framework
statement: Divergent national ICT incident reporting thresholds and taxonomies create multiple overlapping requirements and hinder uniform Union reporting mechanisms, so Regulation 2022/2554 harmonises ICT-related incident reporting through a single streamlined framework for all financial entities, with ESAs specifying taxonomy, timeframes, templates and thresholds.

name: Coordinated resilience testing regime
statement: Because digital resilience testing frameworks are misaligned across subsectors, duplicate costs, hinder mutual recognition and leave vulnerabilities undetected where no testing is required, a coordinated testing regime facilitating mutual recognition of advanced testing is necessary.

name: Third-party contractual weaknesses
statement: Contractual arrangements with ICT third-party providers often lack tailored terms, enforceable access and audit rights, and subcontracting monitoring, and Union outsourcing law does not comprehensively address this external source of ICT risk.

name: Third-party risk principles and contract rights
statement: Key principles for managing ICT third-party risk, with core minimum contractual rights, are needed to let financial entities monitor risk at providers, complementing sectoral outsourcing law.

name: Union Oversight Framework for critical providers
statement: Concentration of financial-sector dependence on a few critical ICT third-party providers poses systemic risk that national mechanisms cannot address, so a Union Oversight Framework with continuous monitoring of critical providers, including cloud providers and complementary to NIS2 supervision, is necessary; intra-group providers are not automatically less risky.

name: Voluntary threat intelligence sharing
statement: Sharing threat and vulnerability intelligence among financial entities improves prevention, containment and recovery, but is inhibited by uncertainty over data protection, antitrust and liability rules; Union-level voluntary sharing arrangements in trusted environments, compliant with competition and GDPR rules, should be enabled.

name: Reporting replaces other regimes
statement: To avoid duplicative obligations, Regulation 2022/2554 reporting replaces PSD2 incident reporting for payment service providers, and its ICT risk obligations replace Chapters III and IV of Directive 2022/2557 for financial entities, since physical resilience is covered.

name: Broad ICT services definition
statement: Regulation 2022/2554 defines ICT services broadly, as digital and data services provided through ICT systems to internal or external users on an ongoing basis (including over-the-top services), excluding only traditional analogue telephone services such as PSTN, POTS and landline services, so that risk from all types of ICT services is addressed.

name: Proportionality by size and risk
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, financial entities must balance resources for ICT risk management against their size, overall risk profile and the nature, scale and complexity of their activities, and competent authorities continue to review this allocation.

name: Scope exclusions and exemptions
statement: Regulation 2022/2554 excludes entities already exempt or lightly regulated under sectoral law (e.g. small AIFMs, certain insurers, tiny pension schemes, small insurance intermediaries, post office giro institutions, entities exempt from Directive 2014/65/EU), while including account information service providers and exempted payment and e-money institutions, and Member States may exempt entities excluded from Directive 2013/36/EU.

name: Simplified framework for small entities
statement: Microenterprises and entities under sectoral light regimes (small non-interconnected investment firms, small pension institutions, exempted payment and e-money institutions) are subject to a simplified ICT risk management framework: they are relieved of complex governance arrangements (third-party monitoring role, control function, annual review, internal audit, crisis function, redundancy, TLPT) and have more flexible testing, while non-exempted payment and e-money institutions follow the general framework.

name: TLPT limited to few entities
statement: Threat-led penetration testing is required only of financial entities meeting the Regulation's criteria, so its costs fall on a small percentage of financial entities; microenterprises and simplified-framework entities are exempt.

name: Management body ultimate responsibility
statement: The management body bears full and ultimate responsibility for ICT risk, must actively steer the ICT risk framework and resilience strategy, cultivate cyber awareness and hygiene among all staff, and secure adequate ICT investment and budget for high digital resilience.

name: Function-based ICT risk framework
statement: Regulation 2022/2554 sets principles inspired by best practice; entities may use differently framed ICT risk models provided capabilities cover identification, protection and prevention, detection, response and recovery, learning and evolving, and communication.

name: Resilient systems and recovery objectives
statement: Financial entities must keep updated, reliable ICT systems with capacity for stressed conditions, and have continuity and recovery plans that resume activity promptly without compromising system integrity or data security; recovery time and point objectives are flexible but must consider impact on market efficiency.

name: Direct reporting to competent authority
statement: All financial entities report major ICT-related incidents directly to their competent authority; where several authorities supervise an entity Member States designate a single addressee, and significant credit institutions report to national authorities which transmit to the ECB.

name: Information flows after incidents
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, financial supervisors receive major ICT incident reports immediately and pass details to non-financial authorities (NIS2 authorities, CSIRTs, data protection and law enforcement), while supervisors give feedback to the entity and the ESAs share anonymised threat data for collective defence.

name: Payment incident reporting irrespective of ICT nature
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, credit institutions, payment institutions, account information service providers and e-money institutions report all operational or security payment-related incidents, previously reported under PSD2, irrespective of whether the incident is ICT-related.

name: Possible single EU Hub
statement: The ESAs, with the ECB and ENISA, are to assess the feasibility of centralising major ICT incident reports in a single EU Hub, either receiving reports directly or coordinating reports forwarded by national authorities.

name: Risk-graduated testing
statement: Financial entities must regularly test ICT systems and staff across preventive, detection, response and recovery capabilities, using a range of tools from basic assessments to advanced threat-led penetration testing (TLPT); TLPT is required only of ICT-mature entities meeting the Regulation's criteria, such as large systemic institutions, and is more relevant for systemic core subsectors.

name: Single home-state TLPT for cross-border groups
statement: Cross-border financial groups comply with one set of TLPT requirements in their home Member State covering ICT infrastructure in all Union jurisdictions, so testing costs arise in one jurisdiction only; Member States may designate a single authority for TLPT matters.

name: TLPT scope, pooling and testers
statement: Financial entities choose which critical or important functions a TLPT covers; pooled testing is permitted only under safeguards when provider services to out-of-scope customers could be affected; internal testers are allowed with supervisory approval, no conflicts of interest and alternation, but threat intelligence providers must be external; responsibility stays with the entity and attestations are not supervisory endorsement.

name: Wide ICT third-party provider coverage
statement: Regulation 2022/2554 covers a wide range of ICT third-party providers, including cloud, software, data analytics and data centre providers, intra-group ICT providers, financial entities serving other financial entities, and payment-processing participants, excepting central banks operating settlement systems and public authorities performing State functions.

name: Retained responsibility and proportionate monitoring
statement: A financial entity remains fully responsible for compliance when using ICT providers, and monitors provider risk proportionately to the nature, scale, complexity and criticality of dependencies and potential impact on service continuity.

name: Third-party strategy and register
statement: Management bodies adopt an ICT third-party risk strategy based on continuous screening of dependencies, and all financial entities maintain a register of information on all ICT service contractual arrangements that supervisors may request.

name: Pre-contract analysis and termination
statement: Before contracting ICT providers, entities analyse criticality, concentration risk, supervisory approvals, due diligence and conflicts of interest; termination may be prompted by serious breaches, performance alteration, provider risk management weaknesses, or inability of supervisors to supervise effectively.

name: Flexible approach to concentration risk
statement: The Regulation addresses ICT third-party concentration risk flexibly and gradually, without rigid caps on exposures, to balance contractual freedom and financial stability; entities assess subcontracting, and Lead Overseers watch for concentration threatening Union financial stability.

name: Harmonised key contract elements
statement: Key contractual elements with ICT providers are harmonised at minimum level so financial entities, deeply dependent on provider ICT services, can fully monitor provider risk; existing contracts are aligned when renegotiated.

name: Critical function definition alignment
statement: The Regulation's definition of 'critical or important function' encompasses critical functions under Directive 2014/59/EU.

name: Core contractual elements for all ICT services
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, all contracts with ICT third-party providers, whatever the criticality of the function supported, must specify functions, services, locations of service and data processing, service levels, data security and availability provisions, data access and return on provider insolvency or discontinuation, incident assistance at no extra or ex-ante cost, cooperation with competent and resolution authorities, and termination rights with minimum notice periods.

name: Additional terms for critical or important functions
statement: Contracts for ICT services supporting critical or important functions must additionally contain full service levels with precise quantitative and qualitative targets, provider notice and reporting duties on developments affecting service, tested business contingency plans and security measures, participation in the entity's TLPT, and access, inspection and audit rights for the entity and its competent authority.

name: Exit strategies and resolution resilience
statement: Contracts must provide dedicated exit strategies with mandatory transition periods enabling switching to other providers or in-house solutions, and financial entities within the scope of Directive 2014/59/EU must ensure ICT contracts are resolution resilient, with non-termination, non-suspension and non-modification clauses on grounds of restructuring or resolution while payments continue.

name: Voluntary standard contractual clauses
statement: Voluntary use of standard contractual clauses developed by public authorities or Union institutions, notably Commission clauses for cloud computing, can increase legal certainty for financial entities and providers.

name: Oversight Framework is sector-specific
statement: Critical ICT third-party providers are subject to a Union Oversight Framework to promote supervisory convergence and financial stability, justified by Union-level added value and the specificity of ICT in finance; it is not a model for Union supervision in other areas of financial services.

name: Designation of critical providers
statement: The Oversight Framework applies only to providers designated as critical using quantitative and qualitative criteria assessed on the entire group structure; non-designated critical providers may opt in voluntarily, while providers already under ESCB oversight, financial entities providing ICT services to other financial entities, intra-group providers, and providers serving only one Member State's domestic entities are exempt.

name: Cyber incidents propagate fast
statement: Reliance of finance on cloud, software and data services makes the ecosystem co-dependent on critical providers, and cyber incidents multiply faster than other risks and across sectors and borders, potentially becoming a systemic crisis, which makes convergent supervision of ICT third-party risk essential.

name: Sanctions for non-cooperation
statement: Because Lead Overseer oversight depends on provider cooperation, access to premises and information, a commensurate sanctioning regime, including penalty payments, is necessary.

name: Union subsidiary for third-country critical providers
statement: To ensure enforceability of penalties and defence rights, a critical ICT provider established in a third country must establish a Union subsidiary within 12 months of designation to keep serving Union financial entities, but this imposes no data localisation and services may be supplied from outside the Union.

name: Third-country oversight powers
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, the Lead Overseer may exercise oversight powers in third countries to examine facilities from which critical ICT providers actually provide or manage services, subject to the provider's consent, notification to and non-objection by third-country authorities, and anchoring in administrative cooperation arrangements concluded by the ESAs, which create no legal obligations for the Union or Member States.

name: Collective Union-level oversight rationale
statement: Uncoordinated, simultaneous audits by numerous national authorities would deny supervisors a comprehensive view of ICT third-party risk and burden providers, so Lead Overseers (ESAs) with powers of investigation, inspection and information access are needed to address the systemic dimension of ICT risk collectively at Union level.

name: Lead Overseer allocation and structure
statement: Any of the three ESAs may be Lead Overseer, assigned by the preponderance of financial entities in its sectors; the Joint Committee ensures cross-sectoral coordination, supported by an Oversight Forum, a joint oversight network, dedicated examination teams per provider, and a single coordination-point legal entity designated by provider groups.

name: Rights of designated providers
statement: Critical ICT providers have procedural rights: a reasoned statement before designation, explanations on impact on out-of-scope customers before recommendations are finalised, and the duty to give a reasoned explanation if not following recommendations, failing which the Lead Overseer issues a public notice of non-compliance.

name: Follow-up of recommendations by authorities
statement: Competent authorities verify compliance with Lead Overseer recommendations in prudential supervision, may require financial entities to take additional measures, may voluntarily consult NIS2 authorities, and must refrain from individual monitoring measures of critical providers, relying on and coordinating with the Lead Overseer.

name: Oversight does not displace entity responsibility
statement: The Oversight Framework does not replace financial entities' own duty to manage ICT third-party risk, including ongoing monitoring of contracts, nor their full responsibility for legal compliance; it also does not prejudice Member States' oversight of providers important only nationally.

name: Oversight funding and delegated standards
statement: Oversight is fully fee-funded by critical providers, with ESA ICT system development funded by Union and national authority contributions; the Commission specifies designation criteria and fees by delegated acts, and the ESAs draft technical standards (regulatory and implementing, including templates for incident reports and the register) applied proportionately.

name: Subsidiarity and proportionality
statement: A high level of digital operational resilience for regulated financial entities cannot be sufficiently achieved by Member States, because it requires harmonising many Union and national rules, so Union action is justified under subsidiarity; Regulation 2022/2554 goes no further than necessary, satisfying proportionality.

name: Consolidation of ICT rules via amendments
statement: Regulation 2022/2554 consolidates ICT risk management provisions scattered across financial acquis (e.g. Regulations 1060/2009, 648/2012, 600/2014, 909/2014, 2016/1011); those acts are amended and the scope of their operational risk empowerments narrowed so that digital resilience provisions are carried over into this Regulation, with ESAs mandated to draft standards updating existing rules.

name: Payment systems cyber risk
statement: Payment systems and payment processing are at the core of the payment chain and strongly interconnected with the financial system, so cyber-attacks on them can severely disrupt key economic functions; this systemic risk should be addressed by harmonised Union rules, the Commission assessing a scope review aligned with the PSD2 review, and Member States may meanwhile draw inspiration from this Regulation.

name: Subject matter of the Regulation
statement: Regulation 2022/2554 lays down uniform requirements on security of network and information systems supporting financial entities' business: ICT risk management, major incident reporting and voluntary cyber threat notification, resilience testing, threat information sharing, third-party risk management, contractual terms, the Oversight Framework for critical ICT providers, and cooperation, supervision and enforcement.

name: Sector-specific act under NIS2
statement: For financial entities identified as essential or important under NIS2 transposition, Regulation 2022/2554 is a sector-specific Union legal act for the purposes of Article 4 of Directive 2022/2555, and it is without prejudice to Member States' responsibility for essential State functions such as public security, defence and national security.

name: Entities in scope
statement: Regulation 2022/2554 applies to credit, payment, e-money, investment, crypto-asset, CSD, CCP, trading venue, trade repository, fund management, data reporting, insurance, pension, rating, benchmark, crowdfunding and securitisation repository entities, collectively 'financial entities', and also to ICT third-party service providers; Member States may exclude certain Directive 2013/36/EU Article 2(5) entities, informing the Commission.

name: Digital operational resilience
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, digital operational resilience is a financial entity's ability to build, assure and review its operational integrity and reliability by ensuring, directly or through ICT third-party providers, the full range of ICT-related capabilities needed to secure the network and information systems supporting continued financial services, including through disruptions.

name: ICT risk definition
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, ICT risk is any reasonably identifiable circumstance in relation to the use of network and information systems which, if materialised, may compromise security of those systems, technology-dependent tools or processes, operations or service provision, by producing adverse effects in the digital or physical environment.

name: Incident and major incident definitions
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, an ICT-related incident is a single or linked series of events unplanned by the entity that compromises network and information system security and adversely affects data availability, authenticity, integrity or confidentiality or services; it is 'major' when it has a high adverse impact on systems supporting critical or important functions. Payment-related incidents are defined likewise whether ICT-related or not, and are major when they have a high adverse impact on payment services.

name: Cyber threat and TLPT definitions
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, a significant cyber threat is one whose technical characteristics indicate potential to cause a major incident; threat-led penetration testing mimics the tactics, techniques and procedures of real threat actors in a controlled, bespoke, intelligence-led red team test of the entity's critical live production systems.

name: Critical or important function
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, a critical or important function is one whose disruption would materially impair the entity's financial performance, or soundness or continuity of services, or whose failure would materially impair compliance with authorisation conditions or financial services law obligations.

name: ICT concentration risk definition
statement: ICT concentration risk is exposure to one or several related critical ICT third-party providers creating dependency such that their unavailability or failure may endanger an entity's critical or important functions, cause large losses, or endanger Union financial stability.

name: Size category definitions
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, a microenterprise is a financial entity (other than trading venues, CCPs, trade repositories, CSDs) with fewer than 10 staff and turnover or balance sheet not above EUR 2 million; a small enterprise has 10 to 49 staff and turnover or balance sheet above EUR 2 million up to EUR 10 million.

name: ICT third-party risk and intra-group providers
statement: ICT third-party risk is ICT risk arising from use of ICT services of third-party providers or their subcontractors, including outsourcing; an ICT intra-group provider is an undertaking in the same financial group or institutional protection scheme providing predominantly ICT services to group financial entities.

name: Proportionality principle
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, financial entities apply the ICT risk management rules in proportion to their size, overall risk profile and the nature, scale and complexity of their services, activities and operations, and competent authorities take this into account when reviewing ICT risk frameworks.

name: Medium-sized enterprise definition
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, a medium-sized enterprise is a financial entity that is not a small enterprise, employs fewer than 250 persons and has annual turnover not above EUR 50 million and/or annual balance sheet not above EUR 43 million.

name: Internal governance and control framework
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, financial entities must have an internal governance and control framework ensuring effective and prudent ICT risk management, and the management body defines, approves, oversees and answers for it, including data-quality policies, clear ICT roles, the resilience strategy and risk tolerance, continuity and recovery plans, audit plans, budget, third-party policy, and reporting channels on third-party arrangements and incidents.

name: Third-party monitoring role and management knowledge
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, financial entities other than microenterprises must establish a role or designate a senior manager to monitor ICT third-party arrangements, and management body members must keep up sufficient ICT risk knowledge and skills through regular training.

name: ICT risk management framework
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, financial entities must have a sound, comprehensive, documented ICT risk management framework protecting all information and ICT assets and physical infrastructure; it is reviewed at least yearly (periodically for microenterprises) and after major incidents or testing/audit/supervisory findings, continuously improved, and provided to authorities on request.

name: Control function and internal audit
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, entities other than microenterprises assign ICT risk oversight to an independent control function, segregate risk management, control and internal audit functions under a three-lines-of-defence or equivalent model, subject the framework to regular internal audit by competent independent auditors, and formally follow up critical audit findings; compliance verification may be outsourced but responsibility stays with the entity.

name: Digital operational resilience strategy
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, the ICT risk framework includes a digital operational resilience strategy setting risk tolerance and impact tolerance, information security objectives and metrics, ICT reference architecture, detection and prevention mechanisms, testing and a communication strategy, and may include a multi-vendor strategy showing third-party dependencies.

name: ICT systems requirements
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, financial entities must use and maintain updated ICT systems, protocols and tools that are proportionate to operations, reliable, of sufficient capacity including peak volumes, and technologically resilient under stress.

name: ICT risk identification
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, financial entities must identify, classify and document ICT-supported functions and assets, map critical assets and their interdependencies, continuously identify risk sources including exposure to other financial entities, identify third-party dependencies, keep inventories updated, review at least yearly, and (other than microenterprises) assess risk upon major changes and legacy systems.

name: Protection and prevention requirements
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, financial entities must continuously monitor and control ICT systems and deploy security policies, procedures, protocols and tools ensuring resilience, continuity, availability and the authenticity, integrity and confidentiality of data at rest, in use and in transit; solutions must secure data transfer and protect against corruption, loss, unauthorised access and data-management and human error.

name: Security policy, access, segmentation and change management
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, the ICT risk framework must include an information security policy, risk-based network management with automated isolation of affected assets and network connections that can be instantaneously severed or segmented to prevent contagion, least-privilege access controls, strong authentication and cryptographic key protection, documented risk-based ICT change management approved by management, and documented patch and update policies.

name: Detection mechanisms
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, financial entities must have regularly tested mechanisms to promptly detect anomalous activities, network performance issues, incidents and potential single points of failure, with multiple layers of control, alert thresholds and automatic alerts, sufficient monitoring resources, and, for data reporting service providers, systems to check trade reports for completeness and errors.

name: ICT business continuity and response
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, financial entities must have an ICT business continuity policy implemented through documented plans ensuring continuity of critical or important functions, rapid incident response and containment, impact estimation and crisis communication; they must do a business impact analysis, ensure redundancy of critical components, test plans at least yearly (including cyber-attack and switchover scenarios for non-microenterprises), and review them in light of test and audit results.

name: Crisis function and loss reporting
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, non-microenterprise financial entities must have a crisis management function, keep accessible records of activity during disruptions, and on request report estimated aggregated annual costs and losses from major ICT incidents (ESA guidelines due by 17 July 2024); CSDs provide continuity test results to authorities.

name: Backup, restoration and redundancy requirements
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, financial entities must document backup policies (scope and minimum frequency based on criticality or confidentiality) and restoration and recovery procedures, maintain backup systems whose activation does not jeopardise security or data integrity, test them periodically, restore on systems physically and logically segregated from the source, and (other than microenterprises) maintain redundant ICT capacities; CSDs must keep a geographically distinct secondary processing site, and CCP recovery plans must enable recovery of all transactions at the time of disruption.

name: Data integrity checks in recovery
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, when recovering from an ICT-related incident financial entities must perform checks and reconciliations, including when reconstructing data from external stakeholders, to maintain the highest level of data integrity and consistency between systems; recovery objectives must ensure agreed service levels are met in extreme scenarios.

name: Learning and evolving requirements
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, financial entities must gather and analyse information on vulnerabilities, threats and incidents, conduct post-incident reviews after major incidents that disrupt core activities (assessing response, forensics, escalation and communication), feed lessons from testing, incidents and supervision continuously into ICT risk assessment and framework reviews, report at least yearly to the management body, run compulsory ICT security and resilience training for all staff, and (other than microenterprises) monitor technological developments.

name: ICT communication requirements
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, financial entities must have crisis communication plans for responsible disclosure of major incidents or vulnerabilities to clients, counterparts and the public, internal and external communication policies differentiating staff roles, and at least one person tasked with implementing the incident communication strategy and public and media function.

name: RTS on ICT risk tool harmonisation
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, the ESAs through the Joint Committee, consulting ENISA, must develop draft regulatory technical standards further specifying ICT security policies, access controls, anomaly detection, business continuity, response and recovery plans, continuity testing and framework review reports, proportionate to entity size and risk profile, for submission by 17 January 2024.

name: Simplified ICT risk management framework
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554 Article 16, small non-interconnected investment firms, exempted payment, e-money and Directive 2013/36/EU institutions and small occupational retirement institutions are not subject to the full ICT risk management rules; they must still keep a documented ICT risk framework, continuously monitor systems, use resilient updated systems, detect anomalies and handle incidents, identify key third-party dependencies, ensure continuity of critical or important functions with backup and restoration, test these regularly, and feed test and incident lessons into risk assessment and staff training. The framework is reviewed periodically and after major incidents, and a review report goes to the competent authority on request.

name: RTS for simplified framework
statement: The ESAs, through the Joint Committee and consulting ENISA, must draft regulatory technical standards, due 17 January 2024, specifying the simplified framework's elements, systems and tools, continuity plan components, continuity testing (including scenarios where a critical function degrades or fails) and review report content, taking into account entity size, risk profile and complexity.

name: Incident management process
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, financial entities must establish an ICT-related incident management process to detect, manage and notify incidents: record all incidents and significant cyber threats, identify and address root causes, set early warning indicators, classify incidents by priority, severity and service criticality, assign roles, plan communication and escalation, inform senior management and the management body of at least major incidents, and have response procedures restoring services securely and in time.

name: Incident and threat classification criteria
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, entities classify incidents by clients, counterparts and transactions affected and reputational impact, duration and downtime, geographical spread (especially more than two Member States), data losses, criticality of services affected, and economic impact; cyber threats are significant based on criticality of services at risk, clients targeted and geographical spread.

name: RTS on incident classification
statement: The ESAs, via the Joint Committee consulting the ECB and ENISA, must draft standards by 17 January 2024 specifying classification criteria, materiality thresholds for major incidents and significant threats, and the criteria and details for sharing reports with authorities in other Member States, taking account of proportionality and the resources of microenterprises and SMEs.

name: Staged incident reporting
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554 Article 19, financial entities submit to the competent authority an initial notification, an intermediate report when the incident's status or handling changes significantly (with updates as needed or on request), and a final report once root cause analysis is complete and actual impact figures replace estimates, using standard templates and containing enough information to judge significance and cross-border impact.

name: Voluntary cyber threat notification and client information
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, financial entities may voluntarily notify significant cyber threats to the competent authority, and must without undue delay inform clients whose financial interests are affected by a major ICT-related incident of the incident and mitigation measures, and potentially affected clients of protection measures against significant cyber threats.

name: Reporting outsourcing and national CSIRT option
statement: Financial entities may outsource incident reporting to a third-party provider but remain fully responsible for fulfilling it; Member States may additionally require reports to also go to NIS2 competent authorities or CSIRTs.

name: Cross-border incident notification by ESAs
statement: After receiving incident details, the ESA and the ECB, consulting ENISA, assess whether a major ICT-related incident is relevant to authorities in other Member States and notify them, with the ECB informing the ESCB on payment system issues, so authorities can protect immediate financial stability; competent authorities of CSD host states are urgently informed where cross-border activity is significant.

name: Reporting standards harmonisation
statement: The ESAs must develop common draft RTS on report content, time limits and significant cyber threat notification content, and ITS on forms, templates and procedures, submitted by 17 July 2024, taking account of entity size and risk and staying consistent with NIS2 reporting.

name: Single EU Hub feasibility report
statement: The ESAs must submit by 17 January 2025 a joint report on a single EU Hub for incident reporting, covering prerequisites, benefits, limitations and risks (including concentration of sensitive information), interoperability, operation, membership, access and set-up costs.

name: Supervisory feedback and entity responsibility
statement: Competent authorities acknowledge each report and may give timely feedback and anonymised intelligence on similar threats, while the entity remains fully responsible for handling incidents; the ESAs publish yearly anonymised aggregated reports and warnings.

name: Testing programme requirements
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, financial entities other than microenterprises must maintain a sound, risk-based digital operational resilience testing programme as part of the ICT risk framework, using independent internal or external testers, procedures to prioritise and remedy findings with internal validation, and at least yearly tests of all ICT systems and applications supporting critical or important functions.

name: Range of ICT tests
statement: The testing programme must provide for appropriate tests such as vulnerability assessments, network security assessments, gap analyses, scenario-based tests, source code reviews where feasible and penetration testing; CSDs and CCPs must run vulnerability assessments before deploying or redeploying applications and infrastructure; microenterprises combine a risk-based approach with strategic planning balancing resources against risk.

name: TLPT frequency and identification
statement: Financial entities identified by competent authorities, on the basis of impact on the financial sector, systemic character and financial stability concerns, and ICT risk profile and maturity, must carry out TLPT at least every three years, a frequency authorities may raise or lower; TLPT covers several or all critical or important functions on live production systems, with scope validated by authorities.

name: TLPT risk control and attestation
statement: Entities must apply risk controls during TLPT, provide authorities with findings summaries, remediation plans and documentation, and receive an attestation enabling mutual recognition between authorities; they remain fully responsible for test impact and for ensuring provider participation.

name: Tester requirements
statement: TLPT testers must be of highest suitability and reputability, have specific expertise in threat intelligence, penetration and red team testing, be accredited or follow codes of conduct, provide independent assurance and hold professional indemnity insurance; internal testers need authority approval, and external testers must be used every three tests, with only external testers for significant credit institutions; contracts must secure sound handling of results; ESAs draft TIBER-EU-based RTS by 17 July 2024.

name: Audit and information security standards for providers
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, financial entities may contract only with ICT providers complying with appropriate information security standards, taking due account of the most up-to-date and highest-quality standards for critical or important functions, and must pre-determine risk-based audit frequency and scope under accepted audit standards, verifying auditors' skills where services are technically complex.

name: Register reporting and notification duties
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, financial entities maintain the register of information at entity, sub-consolidated and consolidated levels, distinguishing arrangements supporting critical or important functions, report at least yearly to competent authorities on arrangements, provider categories and services, and notify authorities in a timely manner of planned arrangements for critical or important functions and when a function becomes critical or important. The ESAs draft implementing standards on register templates by 17 January 2024.

name: Third-party risk strategy policy
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, financial entities other than microenterprises and Article 16 simplified-framework entities adopt and regularly review an ICT third-party risk strategy, including a policy on ICT services supporting critical or important functions applied on individual, sub-consolidated and consolidated bases, with the management body regularly reviewing risks of such arrangements; the ESAs draft technical standards specifying the policy content by 17 January 2024.

name: Exit strategy requirements
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, for ICT services supporting critical or important functions financial entities must have comprehensive, documented, tested and periodically reviewed exit plans, identify alternatives and transition plans to securely transfer services and data to other providers or in-house, and maintain contingency measures, so that exit causes no business disruption, limit on regulatory compliance, or detriment to service continuity and quality for clients.

name: Concentration and subcontracting assessment
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, before contracting for critical or important functions, financial entities assess whether the provider is not easily substitutable or whether multiple arrangements with the same or closely connected providers create concentration, weigh alternatives, assess subcontracting (especially third-country), insolvency law and data recovery constraints, third-country data protection and enforcement, and whether long subcontracting chains impair monitoring and supervision.

name: Written single-document contract
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554 Article 30, the rights and obligations of the financial entity and the ICT third-party provider must be clearly allocated and set out in writing, with the full contract including service level agreements documented in one written document available to the parties on paper or in a durable, downloadable, accessible format.

name: Subcontracting terms and location notice
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, ICT contracts must describe all services and state whether and on what conditions subcontracting of services supporting critical or important functions is permitted, and must specify regions or countries of service provision and data processing and storage, with advance notice by the provider of any intended change of location.

name: Awareness training participation
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, ICT contracts must set the conditions for ICT third-party providers' participation in the financial entity's ICT security awareness programmes and digital operational resilience training.

name: Ongoing monitoring and audit rights
statement: For ICT services supporting critical or important functions, Regulation 2022/2554 requires a right to monitor provider performance on an ongoing basis, including unrestricted access, inspection and audit rights for the entity, appointed third parties and the competent authority (not limited by other contractual terms), the right to agree alternative assurance levels if other clients' rights are affected, full provider cooperation in on-site inspections including by the Lead Overseer, and details of the scope, procedures and frequency of audits.

name: Microenterprise audit delegation
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, a microenterprise and its ICT provider may agree that the entity's access, inspection and audit rights are delegated to an independent third party appointed by the provider, with the entity able to request information and assurance on provider performance from that party at any time.

name: RTS on subcontracting conditions
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554 Article 30(5), the ESAs, through the Joint Committee, must draft regulatory technical standards, due 17 July 2024, specifying the elements a financial entity must determine and assess when subcontracting ICT services supporting critical or important functions, taking into account size, risk profile and the nature, scale and complexity of activities; standard contractual clauses developed by public authorities must be considered in negotiations.

name: Criteria for critical provider designation
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554 Article 31, the ESAs designate critical ICT third-party providers on all of these criteria: systemic impact of a large-scale failure, systemic importance of the financial entities relying on the provider (G-SIIs and O-SIIs and their interdependencies), reliance for critical or important functions including via subcontracting, and low substitutability (lack of alternatives or migration difficulty); criteria apply to the provider's group as a whole, and designation awaits a Commission delegated act specifying the criteria.

name: Designation procedure and Lead Overseer appointment
statement: The ESAs through the Joint Committee, on recommendation of the Oversight Forum, designate critical providers and appoint as Lead Overseer the ESA responsible for the financial entities with the largest share of total assets using the provider; the provider is notified, has 6 weeks to submit a reasoned statement, oversight starts no later than one month after notification, group providers name a coordination point, and the ESAs publish a yearly Union list. Non-listed providers may apply to be designated, with a decision within 6 months.

name: Third-country provider Union subsidiary duty
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554 Article 31(12), financial entities may use a designated critical third-country ICT provider only if it has established a Union subsidiary within 12 months of designation, and it must notify the Lead Overseer of changes to the subsidiary's management structure.

name: Oversight Forum structure and tasks
statement: The Joint Committee establishes an Oversight Forum sub-committee, composed of ESA Chairpersons, high-level national competent authority representatives and observers (Commission, ESRB, ECB, ENISA, NIS2 authorities), which prepares joint positions, yearly assesses oversight results, promotes best practice on concentration risk, submits benchmarks, may consult independent experts, and the ESAs report yearly on the Section's application; the Section is without prejudice to NIS2 and other cloud oversight rules.

name: Lead Overseer assessment of providers
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554 Article 33, the Lead Overseer is the primary point of contact of each assigned critical ICT provider and assesses whether it has comprehensive, sound and effective rules and arrangements to manage the ICT risk it may pose to financial entities, focusing on services supporting critical or important functions. The assessment covers ICT security, availability and continuity requirements, physical security, risk management, governance, incident reporting, data and application portability, testing, audits and use of standards.

name: Annual oversight plan
statement: Based on its assessment and in coordination with the Joint Oversight Network, the Lead Overseer adopts a reasoned individual annual oversight plan for each critical provider, communicating the draft first; the provider may submit within 15 calendar days a reasoned statement on impact on out-of-scope customers. Once plans are adopted, competent authorities may take measures concerning those providers only in agreement with the Lead Overseer.

name: Joint Oversight Network coordination
statement: The three Lead Overseers set up a Joint Oversight Network to ensure consistent oversight approaches, drawing up a periodically revised common oversight protocol for day-to-day coordination, and may call on the ECB and ENISA for ad-hoc technical advice.

name: Powers of the Lead Overseer
statement: The Lead Overseer may request information, conduct investigations and inspections, request follow-up reports on remedies, and issue recommendations on ICT security requirements, conditions that prevent single points of failure and limit concentration risk, and planned subcontracting, including recommending refraining from subcontracting to a third-country subcontractor for critical or important functions when it poses a clear and serious risk to Union financial stability. It must coordinate in the JON, avoid duplicating NIS2 measures, minimise disruption to out-of-scope customers, and consult the Oversight Forum.

name: Periodic penalty payments
statement: Critical providers must cooperate in good faith with the Lead Overseer. If they do not comply with information, investigation or follow-up measures, then after at least 30 days the Lead Overseer imposes a daily periodic penalty of up to 1% of average daily worldwide turnover for up to six months, set by gravity, duration, intent or negligence and cooperation. The penalties are administrative and enforceable, go to the Union budget, and are normally made public. Before imposing them the provider has defence rights, including a hearing and access to the file.

name: Information requests to critical providers
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554 Article 37, the Lead Overseer may require critical ICT providers, by simple request or binding decision, to provide all necessary information, including contracts, policies, audit and incident reports and information on subcontractors. A simple request is voluntary but any reply must not be incorrect or misleading. A decision must cite the legal basis, purpose, information, time limit, periodic penalties and the right of appeal to the Board of Appeal and Court of Justice. The provider remains fully responsible for the accuracy of what it supplies, and the decision is copied to competent authorities and the JON.

name: General investigations
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554 Article 38, the Lead Overseer, assisted by joint examination teams, may investigate critical providers: examine records, take certified copies, summon representatives for explanations, interview consenting persons and request telephone and data traffic records. Investigators act on written authorisation, and the provider must submit to a decision that states purpose, penalties and legal remedies. Competent authorities and the JON are informed in advance.

name: On-site inspections
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554 Article 39, the Lead Overseer, consulting the JON, may enter and inspect any business premises of critical providers, and conduct off-site inspections, covering all ICT systems, networks and data used for services to financial entities. It may seal premises or records as needed, gives reasonable notice unless an emergency or effectiveness prevents it, and informs competent authorities. If a provider opposes an inspection, it is told that competent authorities may require financial entities to terminate their contracts with it.

name: Conditions for third-country inspections
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554 Article 36, where oversight cannot be achieved through the Union subsidiary or Union premises, the Lead Overseer may act on third-country premises used to provide services to Union financial entities, but only if the inspection is necessary, directly related to services to Union entities, the provider consents, and the third-country authority was notified and did not object. The ESAs conclude administrative cooperation arrangements covering coordination, information exchange, notification of infringements, regulatory updates and possible participation of a third-country representative. If the Lead Overseer cannot inspect abroad, it relies on available facts and documents and documents the consequences, which feed into its recommendations.

name: Joint examination teams and recommendations
statement: Under Regulation 2022/2554, the Lead Overseer is assisted by a joint examination team per critical ICT provider, made up of ESA staff and competent authority staff (plus voluntary national authorities) with ICT and operational risk expertise under a Lead Overseer coordinator; within 3 months of an investigation or inspection it adopts recommendations after consulting the Oversight Forum, and may use the provider's certifications and audit reports.

name: Provider response and public disclosure
statement: Within 60 calendar days of receiving Lead Overseer recommendations, a critical ICT provider must notify its intention to follow them or give a reasoned explanation for not doing so; if it fails or the explanation is insufficient, the Lead Overseer publicly discloses the provider's identity and the nature of the non-compliance, limited to what is relevant and proportionate, unless this would cause disproportionate damage or jeopardise financial stability.

name: Last-resort suspension or termination
statement: Competent authorities inform financial entities of risks identified in recommendations, which entities must take into account; if an entity fails to address them, after 60 days' notice and optional NIS2 authority consultation, authorities may as a last resort require temporary suspension or termination of use of a critical provider's service, weighing gravity, duration, weaknesses, financial crime, intent or negligence, and continuity risk, and allowing time for exit strategies; the provider must cooperate fully.

name: Convergence opinions and information to Lead Overseer
statement: Where a critical provider's divergent approach may harm many financial entities and individual warnings fail to give consistent approaches, the Lead Overseer may issue non-binding, non-public opinions to promote convergent follow-up; competent authorities regularly inform the Lead Overseer of their measures, and it may clarify recommendations on request.

name: Oversight fees
statement: The Lead Overseer charges critical ICT providers fees fully covering its oversight expenditure, including joint examination team and independent expert costs, proportionate to the provider's turnover; the Commission sets amounts and payment by delegated act by 17 July 2024.

name: Oversight RTS harmonisation
statement: The ESAs must submit to the Commission by 17 July 2024 draft RTS specifying voluntary designation application information, the content and format of provider information (including subcontracting template), joint examination team composition, and competent authorities' assessment of measures taken on recommendations.

name: International cooperation on ICT third-party risk
statement: The ESAs may conclude administrative arrangements with third-country authorities to foster cooperation on ICT third-party risk and best practices, and every five years jointly submit a confidential report to Parliament, Council and Commission summarising these discussions and implications for financial stability.

name: Information-sharing arrangements conditions
